title: A murder of crows: the strange poetry of collective nouns

body.heading: Names with feathers on
paragraphs: English does not settle for “a group of”. Geese on the ground are a gaggle, but in flight they become a skein. Fish gather in a school, wolves in a pack, and larks rise in an exaltation — a word that sounds exactly like the joy of the thing it describes.
The darker ones are famous: a murder of crows, an unkindness of ravens, a conspiracy of lemurs. And some are pure theatre: an ostentation of peacocks, a dazzle of zebras, a flamboyance of flamingos.

body.heading: Where the fancy ones came from
paragraphs: Many of these terms were collected in the Book of Saint Albans, printed in 1486, which listed the “terms of venery” a well-educated hunter was expected to know. Scholars suspect some were always jokes — wordplay for the hunting lodge rather than serious science.

That suspicion is good news for players: inventing collective nouns has been a parlour game for over five hundred years. Modern additions, like a prickle of porcupines, follow the same rule — the name should paint a picture of the animal's character.

body.heading: Try it: invent your own
paragraphs: Deal out animals and invent the group name each deserves. A group of sloths might be a slow-motion; a group of kittens, a chaos. The test of a good invention is whether a listener smiles and says “oh, that's exactly right”.

For a harder round, use people: a group of teachers, a group of toddlers, a group of grandparents. Five centuries of tradition say you are allowed — encouraged, even — to be a little bit cheeky, as long as you stay kind.

takeaway: Collective nouns are miniature poems: the best ones tell you what the animal is like before you have seen a single one.
